title: Some distinguish free choice broadly taken (intellectual spontaneity) from free choice strictly taken
source_text: XXI. Caeterum inter Doctos illos viros qui liberum & voluntarium confundere videntur, nonnulli sunt qui monent libertatem voluntatis, sive liberum Arbitrium duplici modo sumi, late, scilicet, & stricte. Libertas voluntatis in genere, sive late sumpta, juxta ipsos, nihil aliud est quam τὸ ἑκούσιον νοητικόν, spontaneum intellectuale, id est, spontaneum praeeunte intellectus lumine, vel judicio. Adeoque in hoc proprie consistit generalis ista voluntatis libertas, quod voluntas hactenus Dominium sui actus habeat, ut nequaquam cogi possit, sed pro libito, ex certa ratione, consideratione, aut judicio, sese moveat, & cohibeat, agat, aut non agat.
pass_a_gloss: But among those Learned men who seem to confound the free & the voluntary, there are some who advise that the liberty of the will, or free Choice is taken in a twofold manner, broadly, namely, & strictly. Liberty of the will in general, or broadly taken, according to them, is nothing else than to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, the spontaneous with the light, or judgement of the intellect going before. And so in this properly consists that general liberty of the will, that the will so far has Dominion of its act, that it can by no means be coerced, but at pleasure, from a certain reason, consideration, or judgement, moves itself, & restrains itself, acts, or does not act.
pass_b_english: Among the learned men who seem to confuse the free and the voluntary, some point out that freedom of the will, or free choice, is taken in two ways, a broad one and a strict one.

Freedom of the will in general, or in the broad sense, is for them nothing but to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, spontaneity led by the light or judgement of the intellect. This general freedom of the will properly consists in the will's having mastery over its act to the extent that it can never be forced. Instead it moves or restrains itself, acts or refrains, as it pleases, for some definite reason, consideration or judgement.

choices.why: Pro libito means at one's discretion; it is qualified at once by 'for some definite reason', so it does not mean caprice.
